analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers to arbitrate workplace disputes instead of going to court.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Tens of millions of U.S. workers sign contracts, as a condition of getting or keeping a job, that require them to settle disputes with their employer through private arbitration — one worker, one case, no judge, no class action. This bill would make those forced agreements unenforceable. Workers could still choose arbitration after a dispute arises, but only voluntarily, with written notice and a 45-day waiting period, and employers could not punish anyone for refusing. The bill also restores workers' ability to band together in class or collective actions, reversing the effect of the Supreme Court's 2018 Epic Systems decision as described in the bill's own findings.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — employees and independent contractors — who currently face forced arbitration clauses covering wages, discrimination, harassment, and discharge. The bill's findings say millions of workers are covered and often don't know they've given up their day in court; class actions matter because individual workers usually can't afford to sue alone. Workers would again be able to go to court, join group claims, and sue employers who retaliate against them for refusing to arbitrate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers bound by forced arbitration clauses

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any pre-dispute arbitration agreement requiring arbitration of a work dispute, making it void and unenforceable.

Allows post-dispute arbitration only if it is truly voluntary: no coercion, plain-language written disclosure of rights, a 45-day waiting period with the statute of limitations paused, and written affirmative consent.
Bars employers from retaliating against a worker who refuses to sign an arbitration agreement, and gives workers a private right to sue over retaliation with attorney's fees.

Amends the National Labor Relations Act to prohibit agreements that force workers to waive the right to pursue joint, class, or collective claims, addressing the Supreme Court's Epic Systems ruling described in the bill's findings.
Applies to independent contractors regardless of how they are labeled, and covers domestic workers, groups often excluded from labor law protections.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — particularly large companies in retail, finance, hospitality, and gig work that use arbitration clauses across their workforce — would face more lawsuits and class actions, higher litigation and settlement costs, and the loss of a private, lower-profile dispute system. The private arbitration industry would lose a steady stream of employment cases.

drawbacks.text: Employers' standard objection: arbitration is faster and cheaper than court, and a return to litigation and class actions would raise legal costs — costs that could fall partly on workers through lower wages or fewer jobs, and would weigh hardest on small businesses with thin margins.

Some workers do prefer arbitration's speed and informality over a court case that can take years; the bill keeps that option only after a dispute arises, with a 45-day waiting period, which supporters of arbitration call an obstacle to a legitimate choice.
The bill applies retroactively in the sense that it covers any dispute arising after enactment even under older contracts, which employers warned would create a wave of newly viable claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers the stakes are large: forced arbitration clauses are nearly universal in some industries, and the bill's own findings argue that individual arbitration plus class waivers means most workplace violations go unpunished because one worker alone can't afford to sue. The honest cost is that litigation is slower and more expensive than arbitration for everyone, including workers, and employers would pass some of the added cost on. On balance the bill trades a fast private process that workers rarely chose for a slower public one they can use together.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP committee the same day, the committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the Restoring Justice for Workers Act on May 15, 2019, joined by 18 original cosponsors including independents Bernie Sanders and Angus King and Democrats such as Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker, and Sherrod Brown.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The bill accumulated 19 cosponsors in total — 17 Democrats and 2 independents — and no Republicans.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on forced arbitration clauses kept the status quo: workplace disputes continue to be routed into individual, private arbitration with class-action waivers intact. The private arbitration industry also keeps the revenue those cases generate. Workers who wanted their day in court gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.role: U.S. Senator from Washington; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 19 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill never left committee.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and caucus, which sets the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; with a Republican-held chamber and White House, no forced-arbitration ban advanced in the 116th Congress.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business coalitions
against.what_they_did: Longstanding opponents of limits on employer arbitration clauses, arguing they prefer arbitration's lower cost and predictability over litigation.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or independent — 17 D and 2 I out of 19 — with no Republican support, and the committee and floor calendars were controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would void pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers, forcing employers back into open court where claims are public and can be pursued in groups. Its interest in defeating the bill ran directly against workers' interest in suing.

Employment arbitration is a significant, recurring revenue stream for commercial arbitration firms; the bill would cut off the pre-dispute pipeline of cases. Arbitration would remain available only after a dispute arises, with strict consent requirements.

Arbitration clauses channel disputes to a smaller set of defense counsel; a return to litigation expands work in some ways but also exposes clients to class actions and broader discovery. Their preference for the arbitration status quo runs against workers' access to court.
